strengths: Addresses an interesting and underexplored problem: verifier-free test-time scaling for diffusion-based reasoning models, motivated by a clear gap in prior work (dependence on external verifiers).

Strong diagnostic analysis in Section 5.1 that carefully identifies why naive test-time scaling (BoN with energy or even ground-truth-guided BoN) fails, isolating 'performance-energy consistency' as the key bottleneck — this motivates the proposed LRNCL loss in a principled way.

Extensive ablations disentangling the contributions of LRNCL loss, KL regularization, and hMCTS inference, including a custom performance-energy consistency metric to substantiate claims about the energy landscape quality.

Strong headline empirical results: training only on Maze sizes up to 6x6 and generalizing to 15x15 with 88% success rate, versus near-total failure of the standard diffusion baseline, demonstrating meaningful out-of-distribution generalization.

Reasonably thorough appendix with hyperparameter sensitivity studies (noise scale, inner-loop optimization steps, MCTS start step), extension of hMCTS to conventional noise-predicting diffusion models with external verifiers, and qualitative visualizations.
Clear algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) and reasonably complete method exposition connecting energy-based diffusion, MCTS, and UCB search.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to two synthetic, relatively small-scale reasoning benchmarks (Maze, Sudoku); it remains unclear how well the approach would transfer to more realistic or higher-dimensional reasoning tasks (e.g., graph problems, planning, or language-grounded reasoning), limiting the demonstrated significance/impact.

Sudoku results are comparatively weak (43% vs 30%, and only up to ~40% under ground-truth-guided BoN), suggesting the method's benefits are less robust outside the Maze domain and absolute performance remains low.

The method introduces substantial complexity (LRNCL, KL regularization, hMCTS with multiple hyperparameters: γ, ts, K, Nr, noise scale, etc.), and the paper does not report computational/wall-clock overhead versus BoN or verifier-based baselines, making it hard to judge whether the accuracy gains justify the added inference cost.

No error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported for any of the main tables/figures, so the statistical robustness of the comparisons (especially the ablation differences, some of which are small, e.g., a few percentage points) is unclear.

The 'performance-energy consistency' metric used to support central claims is a custom, self-defined metric without external validation or comparison to standard rank-correlation measures (e.g., Spearman/Kendall), raising some concern about its objectivity.

Baselines are limited essentially to one prior method ([5], Du et al. 2024); no comparison against other recent test-time scaling or search-based diffusion reasoning methods (e.g., MCTS-based diffusion planning cited as [17]) is included in the main results, which weakens positioning relative to the broader literature.

The KL regularization derivation (Eq. 5) is only briefly justified and relies on a stop-gradient trick and a KNN-based entropy estimator without detailed theoretical grounding or ablation of the entropy estimation choice.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: eliminating dependence on external verifiers for test-time scaling of diffusion-based reasoning models, which is a meaningful gap relative to prior work (e.g., Du et al. 2024, Ma et al. 2025) that relies on external verifiers.

Extensive ablation studies are provided (Tables 1-5, Appendix C, D) isolating the effects of LRNCL loss, KL regularization, and different inference strategies (BoN, MCTS, hMCTS), which aids interpretability of the contributions.

Strong headline result on Maze: VFScale solves 88% of 15x15 mazes when trained only up to 6x6, versus near-total failure (6%) for the baseline, demonstrating meaningful out-of-distribution generalization gains.
The proposed performance-energy consistency metric offers a reasonable, quantifiable way to argue that the learned energy landscape is improved by the proposed losses (Table 4).
Reasonable reproducibility effort: architecture details, training configurations, and compute resource reporting are included in the appendix, along with an algorithm box for hMCTS.

Additional experiment (Appendix E) showing hMCTS also benefits conventional (non-energy-based) diffusion models with an external verifier suggests some generality of the inference method beyond the main energy-based setting.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to two small, synthetic grid-based tasks (Maze and Sudoku). Despite the paper's framing around 'System 2' reasoning and LLM-style Chain-of-Thought, there is no evaluation on any task resembling real reasoning problems (math, code, planning with language), which makes the significance and generality of the claims questionable.

The results show unexplained inconsistencies that undermine the narrative: in Table 1 (N=1, no test-time scaling), the full VFScale training method sometimes underperforms its own ablations (e.g., Sudoku D=33: 0.1953 for full model vs 0.4219 for 'w/o LRNCL'), suggesting LRNCL+KL combined can hurt rather than help in some settings, without discussion or explanation.

In Table 5, plain MCTS denoising with VFScale training performs substantially worse than BoN on Sudoku (e.g., N=321: 0.1328 vs 0.3906), which seems to contradict the paper's motivating claim that MCTS enables 'better navigation in the search space.' This large drop is not analyzed or explained, leaving the reader uncertain why hMCTS works when its constituent MCTS component clearly underperforms alone.

No comparison is made against actual external-verifier-based test-time scaling baselines (e.g., a trained reward model or classifier as verifier) on the same tasks. The core claim that a verifier-free approach can match or approach verifier-based scaling is only partially supported via ground-truth-guided BoN, which is an oracle rather than a realistic verifier baseline.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix, despite the stochastic nature of diffusion sampling and negative-sample generation; this makes it hard to assess whether reported gains (some of which are a few percentage points, e.g., Sudoku improvements) are statistically meaningful.

The method introduces substantial complexity and additional hyperparameters (γ in LRNCL, KL regularization weighting, MCTS start step t_s, branching K, rollouts N_r, noise scale), and Appendix C/D show performance is quite sensitive to several of these (e.g., large swings with noise scale and t_s), raising concerns about practical tunability and robustness.

Training cost roughly doubles to triples with the added losses (Appendix B.4), which is not discussed as a limitation nor factored into the compute-matched comparisons against baseline test-time scaling methods.

Overall performance ceiling remains low in absolute terms even with the proposed method (e.g., Sudoku harder dataset saturates below 45% success at large N, and even ground-truth-guided BoN only reaches similar levels), suggesting the fundamental bottleneck may lie elsewhere (e.g., model capacity or task difficulty) rather than being fully resolved by the proposed training/inference innovations, yet the paper frames this as a solved problem.

The writing and figures (especially Fig. 2) are notation-dense and difficult to parse, and several claims (e.g., the necessity of exactly two negatives, the choice of linear regression over more expressive relations) are asserted without strong justification or comparison to alternatives.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: enabling test-time scaling for diffusion-based reasoning without relying on external verifiers, drawing a clear analogy to LLM System-2 reasoning.
The two-pronged solution (training-side LRNCL+KL regularization to improve the energy landscape, inference-side hybrid MCTS) is coherent and each component is separately ablated and justified.
Extensive empirical validation across Maze and Sudoku benchmarks, including out-of-distribution generalization to much larger/harder instances than seen in training (e.g., 6x6 to 15x15 Maze).

Thorough appendix material: hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (noise scale, inner-loop optimization steps, MCTS start step), extension of hMCTS to conventional noise-predicting diffusion models with external verifiers, and a novel performance-energy consistency metric that helps substantiate the claimed mechanism of improvement.
Clear visualizations of qualitative results (Maze paths, Sudoku grids) and quantitative scaling curves (Fig. 3) that support the main claims of improved test-time scalability.
Reasonably good writing and figures (Fig. 2) that make the contrast between prior work and VFScale intuitive.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two synthetic, combinatorial puzzle domains (Maze and Sudoku); it remains unclear how well the proposed training/inference techniques would transfer to more realistic or continuous reasoning tasks, or to larger-scale models.

Some results are internally inconsistent or under-explained: e.g., in Table 1, the full VFScale training method (with both LRNCL and KL) actually underperforms the w/o-LRNCL and w/o-KL variants at N=1 on several Sudoku settings (0.1953 vs 0.4219 and 0.2578 at D=33/29), which is not discussed or reconciled in the text.

Absolute success rates remain modest in several settings (e.g., Sudoku harder dataset caps around 40-43%), and it is unclear how much headroom exists or how the method would scale to even harder/larger instances.

The LRNCL loss design (fitting a line through only three points—positive and two negatives—with a margin hyperparameter γ) is somewhat ad hoc and lacks strong theoretical grounding for why a linear energy-distance relationship is the appropriate inductive bias; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but doesn't explore alternatives empirically.

Comparisons are only made against a single baseline training/inference pipeline from prior work [5]; no comparison to other plausible strong baselines (e.g., learned external verifiers, other search strategies, or LLM-based symbolic solvers) is provided for context on the achieved absolute performance.

No reported variance/error bars or multiple-seed results, despite relatively small per-condition test sets (e.g., N as low as 64 in some Maze settings, inferred from success-rate granularity), raising concerns about the statistical robustness of some reported differences.

Wall-clock / practical compute overhead of MCTS-based inference (beyond NFE matching) is not reported, which is relevant given the noted limitation that MCTS has limited compatibility with parallel computing.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: enabling number-of-sample test-time scaling for diffusion-based reasoning without relying on external verifiers, by leveraging the model's intrinsic energy function.

Extensive empirical evaluation with many ablations in the appendix, including comparisons against a learned external verifier and ground-truth oracle verifiers (sparse and dense), analysis of different monotonic-regression variants (linear/quadratic/rank-based/fixed), sensitivity to the MCTS switch-over step, negative-sample generation strategy, and multi-seed stability analysis.

Strong demonstrated OOD generalization on Maze (88% success on 15x15 mazes when trained only up to 6x6), a substantial improvement over the standard energy-based diffusion baseline which fails almost completely.

The hMCTS inference method is shown to outperform pure BoN and pure MCTS under matched compute (NFE) budgets, and the paper carefully discusses fairness of comparison (same NFE) as well as wall-clock overhead.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility documentation (architectures, hyperparameters, compute resources, training/inference cost tables) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two synthetic, small-scale combinatorial puzzle domains (Maze and Sudoku) directly inherited from Du et al. (2024); no broader or more realistic reasoning benchmarks are tested, which limits the generality of the 'intrinsic reasoning' claims made in the title/abstract.

Absolute performance on Sudoku remains weak even with the proposed method (~43% max success under OOD conditions), suggesting the approach only partially solves the stated problem despite large relative gains.

The Kendall-tau rank correlation results (Appendix Table 19) show the full method's energy-quality correlation turning negative at the final denoising steps (t=8,9: -0.157, -0.309), which is concerning given that these late steps are most critical for final solution selection, and this issue is not adequately explained or reconciled with the paper's central performance-energy consistency claims.

The 'trade-off' explanation for why the full VFScale model sometimes underperforms ablated variants at N=1 (Table 1) reads as a post-hoc rationalization rather than a predicted or principled outcome, weakening confidence in the training objective's design.

The KL regularization incurs a very large training memory overhead on Maze (21-23GB vs 3.4GB baseline) and increased training time, but it is unclear whether baselines were given equivalent additional training compute/steps for a fully fair comparison.

The external-verifier baseline used to argue superiority of the intrinsic energy verifier (Appendix D.1) is a single simple classifier; a more carefully tuned or richer external verifier (e.g., process-reward-model style) might narrow or reverse this gap, so the claim that external verifiers are inherently inferior is not fully substantiated.

Because the same trained energy model is used both to generate and to select/verify samples, there is a risk of self-consistent bias rather than genuine correctness signal, which is not deeply analyzed.

The core technical contribution (two auxiliary losses plus a hybrid BoN/MCTS search schedule) is somewhat incremental relative to the existing energy-based diffusion reasoning literature (Du et al., 2022; 2024), and related work coverage is narrow, missing broader connections to self-rewarding/verifier-free RL and energy-based model literature.
Code/repository link is not actually provided (blanked out) in the submission, limiting verifiability of reproducibility claims despite detailed textual documentation.

strengths: Addresses a conceptually interesting gap: enabling number-of-sample test-time scaling for diffusion-based reasoning without relying on an external, separately-trained verifier.

The paper includes an unusually extensive set of ablations in the appendix (negative-sample generation strategies, alternative monotonic regression forms, switch-over step ts sensitivity, multi-seed stability, comparison to sparse/dense oracle verifiers, extension to conventional noise-predicting diffusion models), which is commendable diagnostic effort.

The narrative in Section 5.1 clearly isolates two separate bottlenecks (energy-landscape quality vs. search efficiency) before proposing targeted fixes for each, which is a reasonably principled problem decomposition.
Reported gains on the 15x15 Maze OOD generalization task are large in relative terms (6% to 88% success) compared to the naively trained/inferred baseline.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to two small, synthetic, grid-based puzzle tasks (Maze up to 15x15, Sudoku). Despite motivating the work with comparisons to LLM System-2/Chain-of-Thought reasoning, no experiments demonstrate the method scales to any realistic reasoning benchmark, leaving the paper's significance and generality unclear.

Absolute performance remains quite low in several regimes (e.g., Sudoku harder dataset success rate tops out around 43%, Maze at grid size 15 tops out at 88% only after extensive extra compute and training cost), which tempers claims of a decisively solved test-time scaling problem.

The 'verifier-free' framing is significantly weakened by Appendix E and the parameterization choice: the intrinsic-energy verifier only works because the model is explicitly parameterized as an energy-based diffusion model; extending hMCTS to conventional noise-prediction diffusion models still requires an external verifier, so the core contribution is somewhat narrower than advertised.

Non-trivial computational overhead is introduced by the proposed training losses (up to 3.5x training time, up to ~7x VRAM increase from LKL on Maze) and by hMCTS at inference (up to 31% slower than BoN at equal NFE), which is a real cost not sufficiently weighed against the accuracy gains in the main text.

Some empirical results are inconsistently favorable and explained post-hoc: the full VFScale model underperforms ablated variants (e.g., 'w/o KL') at N=1 in Table 1, and this is retrospectively justified as an intentional 'sharpness vs. scalability trade-off' without independent evidence that this was a designed rather than observed-then-rationalized effect.

The Kendall-tau consistency results (Table 19) show the correlation between energy and true quality collapsing or turning negative at denoising steps t=8,9, which is not explained and raises questions about the robustness of the central 'performance-energy consistency' claim across the full denoising trajectory.

No comparison against other recent test-time-scaling-for-diffusion baselines cited in Related Work (e.g., Ma et al. 2025, Yoon et al. 2025), nor against non-diffusion reasoning baselines for Maze/Sudoku, leaving the positioning of VFScale's gains against the current state of the art largely untested.

Notation is inconsistent and occasionally confusing between the main text (LMRNCL) and appendix/tables (LRNCL used interchangeably for the same or a related quantity), which hampers clarity and reproducibility of the exact loss formulation.

The tasks and metric (exact-match success rate on procedurally generated puzzles) are quite narrow proxies for 'reasoning,' and it is unclear how the specific innovations (permutation-based negative sampling, linear regression fitting of 3 energy points) would transfer to other domains, limiting the broader impact of the contribution.

strengths: Tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: enabling number-of-sample test-time scaling for diffusion-based reasoning without relying on an external verifier, by using the model's own energy function.

The two proposed training components (MRNCL loss, KL regularization) are intuitive and are shown to meaningfully improve performance-energy consistency (Table 4) and downstream success rates, with clear ablations isolating each component's contribution (Table 3).

The hybrid MCTS (hMCTS) inference strategy is a sensible combination of BoN (broad early exploration) and MCTS (fine-grained late exploitation), and is shown to outperform pure BoN and pure MCTS baselines under matched NFE budgets.

Strong headline results: solving 88% of 15x15 mazes when trained only up to 6x6, versus near-total failure of the baseline diffusion model, demonstrating substantial out-of-distribution generalization gains.

Extensive and thoughtful appendix analyses, including comparisons against learned external verifiers and perfect GT oracles (showing the intrinsic energy verifier nearly matches a dense GT oracle), Kendall-tau rank correlation across denoising steps, ablations on monotonic regression variants (linear vs quadratic vs rank-based vs fixed), negative-sample generation strategies, adaptive switch-over step selection, and multi-seed stability analysis.
Reasonable transparency about computational costs (training time/memory, inference wall-clock) and an explicit fair-comparison protocol (matched NFE) between search strategies.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to two synthetic, small-scale combinatorial tasks (Maze and Sudoku); it remains unclear whether the approach and its claims of "intrinsic reasoning" akin to human System-2 thinking generalize to more realistic or higher-dimensional reasoning problems (e.g., language-based reasoning, planning, or continuous control), which somewhat undercuts the broad framing in the abstract/intro.

Absolute performance on Sudoku remains modest even with the full method (e.g., 43% success under OOD conditions), and Table 1 shows the full VFScale model sometimes underperforms ablated variants or the original model on Sudoku at N=1, which is only partially explained by the naive-inference-vs-scalability trade-off narrative.

The external-verifier comparison (Appendix D.1) uses a single, relatively simple learned classifier as the point of comparison; this may not represent the best possible external verifier (e.g., a properly trained PRM/ORM as in LLM literature), making the "verifier-free is better" claim less conclusive.

hMCTS introduces non-trivial sequential computational overhead (up to ~30% higher wall-clock time than BoN at comparable NFE, per Table 23) and is noted as poorly parallelizable, which is a practical limitation for real-world deployment despite matched-NFE fairness in the main comparisons.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior energy-based diffusion reasoning work (Du et al. 2022/2023/2024): MRNCL is essentially an extension of the existing contrastive loss with a monotonic/linear regression constraint on negatives, and hMCTS is a fairly straightforward BoN+MCTS hybridization rather than a fundamentally new search paradigm.

No comparison to non-diffusion reasoning baselines (e.g., autoregressive/LLM-based chain-of-thought solvers, or classical combinatorial solvers) is provided to contextualize how competitive this verifier-free diffusion approach is against alternative paradigms for the same Maze/Sudoku tasks.

Some hyperparameters (e.g., MCTS switch-over step ts, exploration constant c, noise scale) appear sensitive and require tuning per task (Appendix C, D.3), and while an adaptive ts variant is proposed, its generality across tasks/domains is not thoroughly validated.
